item.content:encoded:
I agree with most of A Random Day's sentiments above, but I want to clarify a bit more about why I upvoted SCP-5555-EX and why I downvoted this.

I believe you're suffering from inverse issues between your two articles. In your original draft, the writing wasn't all that great, but the idea was very focused and constricted. You might recall in our DMs when I was critting SCP-5555-EX that I emphasized cutting certain points out and rewriting things to be more on-point: this was to contract your idea down to a single focus in order to have the reader follow a single line to its logical end (amnesticization causes deja vu; because deja vu is a common phenomenon and you have experienced deja vu…).

However, in this article, your idea is very wild and toys around with numerous different concepts. It jumps from amnesticization and deja vu to XK-Class Scenarios, parallel realities, precognition, and L33T SP34K (which I'm not a fan of personally and find slightly cliche). Nonetheless, the writing in many parts of the article flows like butter, which I find to be very satisfying and I congratulate you for managing to excel in your writing since the last I've looked at it.

My recommendation for this is to keep the original idea and use your new lexicon skills to rewrite the execution of 5555-EX, but not rewrite the idea. Your goal should be to maximize the horror and spell out enough that a reader will be able to dawn upon the conclusion with a bit of thinking, but not spell it outright. If you would like, I can help you more in DMs, since I'm certain you've got all the tools now to make this a stunning article.

item.content:encoded:
The several "layers" of articles make it take far too long to get to the point, especially because each "layer" doesn't really add much and is largely repetetive, then suddenly there's a giant exposition piece at the end that exactly hits that all-too-often poorly executed cliche of "note written in plain language that tells you what you just read." The core idea behind it isn't terrible, but certainly I've seen better executions on the theme of "the foundation created an anomaly" or "real thing is actually an anomaly."

The thing about killing off 14 different universes also feels like overkill nonsense that's supposed to make you go "Woaaaah that's a lot of people they killed, that sure is bad!" and fails miserably. We have no connection to these universes, and killing them off right after introducing them doesn't create any emotional impact.

And as a less important tidbit, I can get behind the O5 council trying to make themselves immortal, but trying to make everyone immortal, especially through anomalous means, is not something I like. Even the end of death canon only had one member of the O5 council actively liking the idea due to an intense fear of dying.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
"Deja vu is actually people recalling amnesticized memories" is a great concept. But the glacial pacing of the article means that I have to wade through paragraphs of clumsy exposition and lines like "All mentions of "Project Immortality" and other actions regarding inter-dimensional analyzing of deaths of alternate individuals are to be expunged from Foundation databases." to get to that point. Then the article throws out the deja vu concept entirely to mash up alternate dimensions, antimemetics, and fake data glitching with over-the-top lines like ALL TH0SE D3ATH5 F0R N.THI1NgG (leetspeak should also be left in the past) to create buildup that has no mood, atmosphere, or tension. The ending is a confusing, disjointed exposition dump about evil Overseers and multiverse genocide that has zero weight or catharsis and feels utterly disjointed from the rest of the article.

I strongly encourage that this be rewritten again. The Overseer soul-map story needs to be thrown out entirely — it's meandering, poorly explained, disjointed, and clumsily pieced together through an exposition dump badly bolted onto the SCP format. Paul Verlaine isn't a character at all — he's a name that's dropped into the article without significance or meaning. A good rewrite of this article would explore the relationships between memory, reality and false recollections, and engage with how easy it is for a person to rewrite their own past simply because it's all filtered through memory. Maybe Paul Verlaine could be the original test subject for the Foundation's first amnestics — over time, as they amnesticize him and feed him false memories, something starts to happen so that his memories start to become everyone else's. There's a lot of different character-driven avenues to explore, and the nature of memory is an inherently rich topic to mine for horror. As it is, this piece is simply too high concept for its own good.

I met a traveller from an antique land,
Who said—“Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert… . Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed;
And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away.”

- Percy Bysshe Shelley, Ozymandias
